scope: Recall the trade-off table for AM, DSB-SC, SSB-SC and VSB, and know why vestigial sideband exists.
concept: **The one-line picture.** All four schemes are linear (amplitude) modulation: the message spectrum is translated around the carrier, and only the question of *which* parts are transmitted changes. AM sends carrier plus both sidebands; DSB-SC sends both sidebands only; SSB-SC sends one sideband; VSB sends one complete sideband plus a narrow **vestige** (a tapering remnant) of the other. Nothing is gained in noise performance by removing the carrier or a sideband — the benefit is purely in transmitted power and occupied bandwidth, at the cost of receiver complexity.

formulas.n: Simplest receiver (envelope detector, carrier-derived AGC). Standard for medium-wave broadcast.
Carrier suppressed by a balanced modulator; requires coherent detection; saves power but no bandwidth.
One sideband; product detector plus BFO; HF voice, marine, point-to-point. Peak envelope power rating.
One full sideband plus a vestige of the other; used for analogue TV video and some data links.
Vestigial symmetry. It is what makes distortionless detection possible with a simple envelope detector.

formulas.q: Power and bandwidth comparison at m = 1
formulas.n: AM : DSB-SC : SSB-SC. Savings versus AM: 4.77 dB and 7.78 dB respectively.
A transmitted (or reinserted) carrier is what makes envelope detection possible.
Wide enough to cover the lowest message frequency; TV video uses 0.75 MHz of a 4.2 MHz baseband.
VSB saves about 1.25 MHz per channel compared with DSB and allows an envelope detector in a cheap receiver.
DSB-SC has a quadrature null at 90 degrees; SSB shifts all audio by the BFO error in hertz.

formulas.q: Why VSB instead of SSB for video
formulas.e: \mathrm{SSB\ filter\ at\ } f_c\ \mathrm{with\ baseband\ to\ DC\ is\ unrealisable}
formulas.n: Video has significant energy near DC, so the sidebands touch at the carrier and no practical filter can separate them.

traps: **Treating VSB as 'SSB with a bit of the other sideband left over by accident'.** The vestige is deliberate and the filter is designed so that $H(f_c-f)+H(f_c+f)$ is constant across it. Remove the vestige, or filter it asymmetrically, and the envelope-detected video is distorted.

**Claiming SSB is 'twice as efficient in power' as DSB-SC.** SSB is half of DSB-SC in power and half in bandwidth; versus AM at $m=1$ it is a quarter of the power ($7.78\ \mathrm{dB}$) and half the bandwidth. Mixing the baselines produces wrong dB figures.

**Assuming removing the carrier improves the *noise* performance.** Carrier suppression saves transmitted power and nothing else; the post-detection SNR at equal received sideband power is unchanged. Noise performance is a property of the modulation *type* (linear versus angle), not of which sidebands are kept — compare with [[10_AM_vs_FM_Noise_Comparison]].

**Forgetting that VSB still needs a small carrier.** VSB is normally transmitted with a carrier (or a pilot) so that a simple envelope detector works; that is why its power efficiency is close to AM's rather than SSB's.
**Using the wrong bandwidth for VSB.** $BW = W + f_v$, not $W$ and not $2W$: one full sideband of width $W$ plus a vestige $f_v$ on the other side of the carrier.
